lessons.title: Separable verbs — the prefix flies to the end
lessons.summary: Half the verb breaks off and waits at the very end of the sentence — so you cannot know what a German verb means until you hear the last word.
lessons.rule:
A prefix is a small piece stuck onto the front of a verb that changes what it means. stehen means to stand. Put auf in front and aufstehen means to get up. Same core verb, completely different action. rufen is to shout; anrufen is to phone someone.

Now the German twist. In a normal statement — a main clause, meaning a chunk that could stand alone as a complete sentence — that prefix does not stay attached. The verb splits in two. The conjugated half (the half that changed to match the person: ich stehe, du stehst) stays in position 2 where verbs always are, and the prefix flies all the way to the end of the sentence:
aufstehen → Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
anrufen → Ich rufe dich heute Abend an.
einkaufen → Wir kaufen am Samstag ein.

This has a real consequence for listening: you cannot understand a German sentence until you have heard the last word. Ich rufe meine Mutter… is not finished — with an at the end it means I am phoning her, without it, I am shouting for her. Turkish speakers have an advantage here, because you are already used to waiting until the end of a sentence for the verb. Do exactly that in German: the final word is very often the half that carries the meaning.

Which prefixes split? A reliable rule of thumb: if the prefix is also a word you already know on its own, it splits. If it is a meaningless syllable, it never moves. Your ear can decide it too — separable prefixes are stressed: AUFstehen, ANrufen. Inseparable ones are not: beSUchen, verKAUfen.

  • Separable (these fly to the end): auf- an- aus- ein- mit- ab- zu- vor- nach- zurück- weg-
  • Inseparable (these never move): be- ge- er- ver- ent- emp- miss- zer-

Two situations keep the verb in one piece. After a modal verb like müssen or können, the second verb goes to the end whole and unchanged: Ich muss um sieben Uhr aufstehen. And the dictionary form is always written joined. In the past tense the two halves grip a ge between them: aufgestanden, angerufen, eingekauft.

examples.de: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
examples.note: stehe is the conjugated half and sits in position 2; auf has to wait until the end.

examples.de: Ich rufe dich heute Abend an.
examples.note: Three words stand between the two halves of anrufen. The prefix is still the last thing said.

examples.en: Are you coming along this evening?
examples.note: In a yes/no question the verb starts the sentence, but the prefix still closes it.

examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.
examples.note: After a modal verb the second verb goes to the end in one piece — no splitting at all.

examples.de: Wir kaufen am Samstag im Supermarkt ein.
examples.en: We do the shopping at the supermarket on Saturday.
examples.note: Without the final ein this would mean we are buying something, not doing the weekly shop.

examples.de: Ich besuche am Wochenende meine Eltern.
examples.en: I'm visiting my parents at the weekend.
examples.note: be- is not a word on its own, so besuchen never splits. Nothing goes to the end.

mistakes.right: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
mistakes.why: You cannot conjugate the whole block. The personal ending goes on stehen, and the prefix is pushed out to the end of the sentence.
The prefix is not glued to the verb the way English keeps 'call up' together. It has to travel past everything else and be the final word.
Only one verb in the sentence gets a personal ending, and that is muss. The second verb goes to the end unchanged and unsplit.

mistakes.wrong: Ich hole dich um acht Uhr.
mistakes.right: Ich hole dich um acht Uhr ab.
mistakes.why: Forgetting the prefix changes the meaning, it does not just sound odd — holen alone means to fetch something, abholen means to pick a person up.

drills.question: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr ___.
drills.explain: The conjugated half stehe is already in position 2, so only the bare prefix is left over for the end.

drills.question: Which sentence is correct?
drills.explain: The personal ending belongs on rufen, and the prefix has to move past the object and the time word to the last slot.

drills.question: Der Film fängt um acht Uhr ___. (anfangen)
drills.explain: anfangen splits, and in a statement nothing at all may stand after the prefix.

drills.question: Which of these verbs does NOT split?
drills.explain: be- is a meaningless syllable rather than a word of its own, and those prefixes stay attached forever.

drills.question: Wir kaufen am Samstag im Supermarkt ___. (einkaufen)
drills.explain: Even with a time and a place in between, the prefix still lands after all of them.

drills.question: Ich muss morgen früh ___.
drills.explain: A modal verb sends the second verb to the end as one unsplit, unchanged word.

drills.answer: Ich hole dich um acht Uhr ab
drills.explain: abholen splits: hole takes position 2 and ab is squeezed out to the very last place.
A yes/no question starts with the verb, but that does not rescue the prefix — it still finishes the sentence.

lessons.title: Perfekt — how Germans talk about the past
lessons.summary: Two pieces: haben or sein in position 2, and the frozen participle form at the very end of the sentence.
lessons.rule:
When a German tells you what they did yesterday, they use the Perfekt. This is the everyday past tense of spoken German — for holidays, for work, for what you had for lunch. Turkish does this with one word and a suffix (gittim). German needs two pieces, and they end up at opposite ends of the sentence.

Piece one is a helper verb — a verb that carries no meaning of its own and is only there to hold the grammar. German has exactly two: haben or sein. It is conjugated normally and sits in position 2, where the verb always is. Piece two is the past participle: one fixed form of the real verb that never changes for person, and it is parked at the very end of the sentence. Everything you want to say gets sandwiched in between:
Ich habe gestern Abend einen Film gesehen.

Building the participle. Regular verbs take ge + the stem + t: machen → gemacht, kaufen → gekauft, spielen → gespielt. Irregular verbs take ge + the stem + en, usually with a vowel change inside: gehen → gegangen, sehen → gesehen, trinken → getrunken. There are around a hundred common irregular ones and they have to be learned one by one, like English go / gone.

Two groups take no ge at all: verbs ending in -ieren (studieren → studiert, telefonieren → telefoniert) and verbs with an inseparable prefix (besuchen → besucht, verkaufen → verkauft). Separable verbs are the opposite — the ge slots into the middle: aufstehen → aufgestanden, einkaufen → eingekauft.

Now the choice that worries everybody: haben or sein. About nine verbs in ten take haben, so make that your default. Use sein when the verb is movement from A to B (gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen, laufen) or a change of state, where you are one thing before and something else after (aufstehen, einschlafen, werden, sterben) — plus the two odd ones you simply memorise, sein and bleiben. English gives you no help here at all, since English uses have for everything.

tables.title: haben or sein?
rows: machen, essen, sehen, kaufen, arbeiten, schlafen

tables.title: The bracket — helper second, participle last

examples.de: Ich habe gestern einen Film gesehen.
examples.note: habe in position 2, gesehen as the final word, everything else in the gap between them.

examples.de: Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?
examples.en: What did you do at the weekend?
examples.note: The question you will hear every Monday. machen is regular: ge + mach + t.

examples.de: Wir sind mit dem Zug nach Köln gefahren.
examples.en: We went to Cologne by train.
examples.note: fahren takes you from one place to another, so the helper is sein, not haben.

examples.de: Ich bin um sechs Uhr aufgestanden.
examples.note: A separable verb puts ge in the middle, and getting up is a change of state, so sein.

examples.de: Ich habe zwei Jahre in Istanbul studiert.
examples.en: I studied in Istanbul for two years.
examples.note: Verbs in -ieren never take ge. It is studiert, never gestudiert.
Eating is not movement, so haben — and essen is irregular, giving gegessen.

mistakes.why: fahren moves you from one place to another, and movement verbs take sein. English 'have' is no guide, because English uses have for everything.

mistakes.wrong: Ich habe gestern gesehen einen Film.
mistakes.right: Ich habe gestern einen Film gesehen.
mistakes.why: English keeps the verb and its object side by side. German throws the participle to the very end and stacks everything else in front of it.
Verbs ending in -ieren drop the ge completely. The same goes for besucht, verkauft and bezahlt.

mistakes.wrong: Ich habe gestern zu Hause geblieben.
mistakes.right: Ich bin gestern zu Hause geblieben.
mistakes.why: bleiben means staying still, so it looks like a haben verb, but it is one of the fixed exceptions that take sein — just like sein itself.

drills.question: Ich ___ gestern einen Film gesehen.
drills.explain: Watching is neither movement nor a change of state, so it falls into the big haben group.

drills.question: Ich ___ nach Berlin gefahren.
drills.explain: fahren carries you from one place to another, and movement always picks sein as its helper.

drills.question: Was hast du gestern ___? (machen)
drills.explain: machen is regular, so the recipe is ge in front and t at the end.

drills.question: Ich habe zwei Jahre in Istanbul ___. (studieren)
drills.explain: Verbs ending in -ieren are the one group that never gets a ge in front.

drills.question: Wir ___ um sechs Uhr aufgestanden.
drills.explain: Getting up turns you from lying down into standing, and that change of state takes sein.

drills.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: Ich habe gestern gekauft ein Buch.
Ich habe gestern ein Buch gekauft.
Ich habe gekauft gestern ein Buch.
drills.answer: Ich habe gestern ein Buch gekauft.
drills.explain: The participle has to be the last word, so the time and the object are both pushed in front of it.

drills.answer: Ich habe gestern Abend einen Film gesehen
drills.explain: Helper in position 2, participle last, and all four words of detail sandwiched between them.

drills.answer: Wir sind mit dem Zug nach Köln gefahren
drills.explain: sein is the helper because of the movement, and gefahren still has to close the sentence.

lessons.title: Präteritum — the written past
lessons.summary: A one-word past you mostly need to recognise in writing — except for war, hatte and the modals, which you will say every single day.
lessons.rule:
German has a second past tense: the Präteritum. It is one word instead of two — ich ging where the Perfekt says ich bin gegangen. Both mean exactly the same thing, I went. The difference is not meaning. It is where you are allowed to use them.

Präteritum lives in writing: novels, newspapers, reports, the news on television, fairy tales. Perfekt lives in speech. If you say Ich ging gestern ins Kino to a colleague at lunch, you sound like a man reading aloud from a book. Say Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen. So for most verbs, this lesson is a recognise it lesson — you need to understand er sah, sie kam, er sagte on a page, and never produce them yourself.

But there is a small group that goes the other way. These use the Präteritum even in conversation, and using the Perfekt for them sounds clumsy and foreign. This group you must produce, actively, from day one:

  • sein → war: Ich war gestern nicht im Büro.
  • haben → hatte: Ich hatte keine Zeit.
  • the modals: können → konnte, müssen → musste, wollen → wollte, dürfen → durfte, sollen → sollte
  • es gibt → es gab: Es gab ein Problem.

How the forms are built, for reading. Regular verbs push -te- in before the ending: machen → ich machte, du machtest, er machte. Irregular verbs change the vowel and add nothing: gehen → ging, kommen → kam, sehen → sah, fahren → fuhr. The one thing that always gives it away: in the Präteritum, ich and er/sie/es are identical — ich war / er war, ich ging / er ging. There is no -t on the third person the way there is in the present.

One trap worth marking now. konnte and könnte are two different words, and so are musste and müsste. The plain vowel is the past: I could / I had to. The two dots make it a polite or hypothetical form: I would be able to / I would have to. In the past there is never an umlaut.

tables.title: sein and haben — learn these cold
The modals in the past — no umlaut
Which past do Germans actually say?
headers: In a book or the news

examples.de: Ich war gestern nicht im Büro.
examples.en: I wasn't at the office yesterday.
examples.note: The normal spoken past of sein. Ich bin gewesen exists, but almost nobody says it.
haben also stays in the Präteritum in speech — hatte with the du ending -st.

examples.de: Ich konnte gestern leider nicht kommen.
examples.note: Modals in the past are always Präteritum in conversation. Note the plain o, not ö.
es gibt becomes es gab. You will need this in every shop and every office story.

examples.en: We had to wait for an hour.
examples.note: mussten, no umlaut. müssten would mean we would have to.

examples.de: Er ging langsam nach Hause. Niemand sah ihn.
examples.en: He walked slowly home. Nobody saw him.
examples.note: Two Präteritum forms in a row — this is narration. Out loud you would say: Er ist nach Hause gegangen.

mistakes.wrong: Ich bin gestern sehr müde gewesen.
mistakes.why: The Perfekt of sein is not broken grammar, it is just wrong for conversation. sein is one of the few verbs that stays in the Präteritum when you speak.

mistakes.right: Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen.
mistakes.why: gehen is an ordinary verb, so its Präteritum belongs in books and news reports. In speech every ordinary verb uses the Perfekt.
Modals go the opposite way to normal verbs: the one-word past is what people say, and the Perfekt form sounds heavy and unnatural.
The two dots change the word. konnte is the past, könnte means 'I would be able to' and points at the future, so with gestern it contradicts itself.

drills.question: Gestern ___ ich sehr müde.
drills.explain: sein is one of the handful of verbs whose one-word past is the normal spoken form.

drills.question: ___ du gestern Zeit? (haben, Präteritum)
drills.explain: haben also stays in the Präteritum in speech, and du adds -st to the hatte stem.

drills.question: Ich ___ gestern leider nicht kommen.
drills.explain: gestern fixes this in the past, and the past form of können has no umlaut.

drills.question: Which sentence would you actually say to a colleague?
options: Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen.
Ich war gestern ins Kino gegangen.
drills.answer: Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen.
drills.explain: gehen is an ordinary verb, so spoken German reaches for the two-piece Perfekt, not the written one-word past.

drills.question: Wir ___ eine Stunde warten. (müssen, Präteritum)
drills.explain: Modals use the one-word past in speech, and wir takes the plural ending -en on the musste stem.

drills.question: Gestern ___ ein Problem mit dem Zug.
drills.explain: es gibt becomes es gab in the past, and because Gestern already fills position 1 the verb has to come before es.
One word does the whole past here, so the verb sits alone in position 2 with nothing waiting at the end.

drills.answer: Wir waren letztes Jahr in Berlin
drills.explain: The wir form of war adds -en, and no participle is needed because sein does not use the Perfekt in speech.
